analysis.one_liner: Gives young immigrants brought to the U.S. as children a path to permanent legal status.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2019 by a Republican and a Democrat together, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day and never received a committee vote or floor action before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let people who were brought to the United States as children stay permanently and eventually apply for citizenship. It covers those who have lived here at least four years, entered before age 18, stayed out of serious criminal trouble, and are in school, have a diploma or GED, or are pursuing higher education. People already in the DACA program, which shields from deportation those brought here as kids, would qualify automatically unless they later did something disqualifying. The bill also restores states' power to let undocumented students pay in-state college tuition.
analysis.who_benefits: Young immigrants who entered the United States as children and their families: they could stop fearing deportation, work legally, attend college, and eventually naturalize. DACA recipients gain a permanent solution instead of a program that depends on each administration's discretion.

how_it_helps.text: The Department of Homeland Security must cancel removal and grant conditional permanent resident status to anyone present in the U.S. for four years who entered before age 18, is not barred for crime or security reasons, and meets education requirements (admitted to college, a high school diploma or GED, or currently enrolled in school or an education program).
People granted DACA status are automatically adjusted to conditional permanent residence unless they have since engaged in conduct that would make them ineligible for DACA.
The bill bars the government from using information in applications, or in DACA requests, for immigration enforcement, and forbids referring applicants to ICE or Border Protection.
Applicants still in elementary or secondary school (age 5 or older) get a stay of deportation and a work permit while they remain enrolled.
The bill repeals a 1996 federal restriction, letting states offer in-state tuition and other higher education benefits to undocumented students.

analysis.who_pays: Applicants who aren't exempt pay processing fees, and taxpayers fund the background checks, medical exams, and processing. Critics of any legalization argue the country absorbs the cost of regularizing people who entered unlawfully; supporters note applicants are screened, fingerprinted, medically examined, and must register for selective service.

drawbacks.text: Eligibility is narrower than the population of people brought here as children: those without a diploma or GED, not enrolled in school, and not admitted to college do not qualify at all, and criminal bars are broad.

Permanent status is not immediate. Conditional residence lasts up to eight years, and removing the conditions requires a college degree, at least two years of college, two years of military service, or roughly three years of steady employment.

The core objection from opponents is that it grants permanent residency to people who entered or remain in the country unlawfully; the bill itself applies to people who are inadmissible or deportable under current law.

Applicants must pay a processing fee unless they qualify for exemptions (minors under 18 who are low-income and in foster care or homeless, people with serious disabilities, or those with large medical debt).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people covered, the bill's benefits are life-changing: legal status, work authorization, protection from deportation, and eventual citizenship. The trade-offs are real but modest — a long conditional period with work or education requirements, fees for many applicants, and a narrower scope than the full population of childhood arrivals. The fundamental dispute is not design but principle: opponents reject legalizing anyone who entered unlawfully, so no version would have satisfied them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never got a committee vote or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Lindsey Graham introduced the bill for himself and Senator Dick Durbin on March 26, 2019.
Five senators cosponsored it: three Democrats and two Republicans.

The Senate's only action was to read it twice and refer it to the Committee on the Judiciary; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote through the end of the Congress in January 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Young immigrants, including DACA recipients, got no relief and kept living without permanent status. Senators who opposed a citizenship path were spared a vote on one with bipartisan sponsorship, and the enforcement-only status quo they preferred continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of legalization; Dreamers left waiting

for.role: U.S. Senator from South Carolina and lead sponsor

for.name: Dick Durbin

for.name: Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing on both sides.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill after its referral to Judiciary.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Republican lead sponsor working with the Democrats' lead sponsor, plus three Democratic and two Republican cosponsors — but no vote was ever held to test where the full Senate stood.

industries.note: The bill repeals the 1996 ban on states offering undocumented students in-state tuition, and a large share of eligible applicants must pursue or complete higher education to keep permanent status, adding enrolled students. The benefit to schools runs alongside the benefit to the students themselves.

Legalized workers get employment authorization, including work permits for school-age applicants whose removal is stayed, giving employers a larger documented workforce and workers protection from being paid under the table.
